It was not the surveyor who was at fault, and it was not the master.
What makes it law in any particular ship is ratification by the state whose flag she flies.
The classification society to which the owner had contracted the surveys held one authorisation only.
The port authority in whose waters she lay was acting for a different state.
A convention does not become law because it is adopted.
What produced the detention was an amendment that one registry had accepted and the other had not.
The port authority in whose waters she lay was acting for a state which had ratified both instruments.
Liability did not follow the fault; it followed the flag.

I have been asked the same question by three different lawyers, and the answer has not changed. I surveyed that vessel against the regime her flag state had accepted, because that is the only regime I am authorised to survey her against. My authorisation comes from one administration and from no other. If a port on the far side of an ocean has ratified a protocol that her registry has not, that is not a defect in my survey and it is not something I am permitted to correct. What people find hard to accept is that both certificates in that argument were valid. Mine was valid under the law that appointed me. Theirs was valid under the law that controlled the water. It was the water that won, and it always is.

There are three steps and most people only know the first. A convention is adopted at the organisation, and that is the photograph everybody has seen. Then it has to be ratified, which means each state accepts to be bound by it, and the instrument only enters into force once enough of them have done so. And then, third, it has to be transposed: written into the national law of that state, with a penalty attached. A state can complete step two and never complete step three, and when that happens you have a convention that is technically in force and practically invisible. It is enforcement, not ratification, that decides what a master actually experiences. Which is why the interesting question about any flag is never what it has signed. It is what it has ever detained a ship for.
